title: RESTCONF Protocol
summary: Describes an HTTP-based protocol that gives a programmatic interface for accessing data defined in YANG, using the datastore concepts from NETCONF. It lets tools manage network devices with ordinary web-style requests.

eli5.summary: Instead of special tools, you manage a network device with the same kind of web requests a browser uses. This sets the rules for it.

questions: how does restconf find the api root
what http methods does restconf use
subtitle: Manage a network device's YANG-modeled configuration and state with ordinary HTTP requests carrying XML or JSON.

tldr.problem: Web applications need a standard, modular way to reach the configuration data, state data, RPC operations and event notifications inside a networking device.
tldr.mechanism: RESTCONF maps HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) onto create, read, update and delete operations on YANG-defined data, using NETCONF datastore concepts, with XML or JSON message bodies over TLS.
tldr.outcome: A client that knows a server's YANG modules can derive every resource URL and request format. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8527.

today: RFC 8040 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8527, so read the two together. It has not been obsoleted by the metadata available here.

sections.title: What RESTCONF Is
sections.content:
There is a need for standard mechanisms that let web applications reach the configuration data, state data, data-model-specific remote procedure call (RPC) operations and event notifications inside a networking device, in a modular and extensible way. RESTCONF is a protocol based on HTTP (RFC 7230) for configuring data defined in YANG version 1 (RFC 6020) or YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950), using the datastore concepts of NETCONF (RFC 6241).

Configuration and state data are exposed as resources. They can be read with GET, and configuration resources can be changed with DELETE, PATCH, POST and PUT. Data is encoded as XML or JSON, and YANG rpc and action operations are invoked with POST.

RESTCONF implements a subset of NETCONF, for instance by eliminating datastores and explicit locking. It is not meant to replace NETCONF, but to give an HTTP interface that follows REST principles and stays compatible with the NETCONF datastore model.
sections.eli5: A network device has a big settings list. RESTCONF lets a web program read and change that list using the same kind of requests a browser uses to load pages.

sections.title: A Data-Model-Driven API
sections.content:
RESTCONF combines the simplicity of HTTP with the predictability of a schema-driven API. Knowing the YANG modules a server uses, a client can derive all management resource URLs and the structure of every request and response. This removes the need for HATEOAS links in responses, because the client can work out the links it needs from the YANG modules.

The server MUST implement the ietf-yang-library module (RFC 7895), which MUST identify all YANG modules the server uses. Whether data is configuration or state comes from the YANG config statement, and ordering comes from ordered-by.

The editing model is simple and direct, like the NETCONF :writable-running capability: each edit is activated when it completes successfully.

When a RESTCONF server runs on a device that also has a NETCONF server, edits go to the running datastore if :writable-running is supported, otherwise to the candidate datastore, which MUST be committed immediately. If :startup is supported, the startup datastore MUST be updated after each edit. If a NETCONF client holds a lock on the datastore, the RESTCONF edit MUST fail with 409 Conflict and error-tag in-use.
sections.eli5: Because the device publishes a map of everything it has, a program can figure out the right web address for any setting without being told.

sections.title: Transport and Authentication
sections.content:
RESTCONF requires that the transport provide data integrity and confidentiality. A server MUST support TLS (RFC 5246) and SHOULD adhere to RFC 7525, and the protocol MUST NOT be used over HTTP without TLS. At least HTTP/1.1 is RECOMMENDED. Implementations MUST support the https URI scheme, whose default port is 443.

Servers MUST present an X.509v3 certificate. The client MUST either validate the certificate path (RFC 5280) or match it against a certificate obtained by a trusted mechanism, such as a pinned certificate. If neither succeeds, the connection MUST be terminated. The client MUST also check the server identity as in Section 3.1 of RFC 2818.

The server MUST authenticate client access to any protected resource, and SHOULD answer an unauthenticated client with 401 Unauthorized. It SHOULD require TLS client certificates; if that is not feasible, HTTP authentication MAY be used. The resulting identity, the RESTCONF username, is subject to the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 6536).
sections.eli5: All the talking happens in a locked, secret tunnel, and both sides check who the other is before anything private is shared.

sections.title: Resources and Their URIs
sections.content:
RESTCONF works on a hierarchy of resources starting with the top-level API resource. A client first finds the API root by getting /.well-known/host-meta and reading the single restconf link relation; for example the root might be /restconf. That root is written {+restconf} in the RFC. Because of this discovery method, one endpoint (host and port) can support only one RESTCONF server.

  • {+restconf}/data: the mandatory datastore resource, holding combined configuration and state data. The client cannot create or delete it.
  • {+restconf}/operations: an optional container giving access to data-model-specific RPC operations.
  • {+restconf}/yang-library-version: a mandatory leaf with the revision date of the ietf-yang-library module.

A data resource is a YANG data node below the datastore, such as a container, leaf, leaf-list entry or list entry. Its URI is built left to right from the top-level node, with module-name: prefixed when the module changes. List keys follow the list name after =, separated by commas, with reserved characters percent-encoded, for example list1=key1,key2,key3.

The other resource types are operation resources (invoked with POST), an optional schema resource for fetching YANG modules, and event stream resources. The two media types are application/yang-data+xml and application/yang-data+json.
sections.eli5: Everything on the device has its own web address, like folders inside folders. You follow the path to the setting you want.

sections.title: Methods and Query Parameters
sections.content:
HTTP methods identify the create, read, update and delete action. A server MUST support OPTIONS, HEAD, GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and PATCH (plain patch).

  • GET retrieves data and metadata; a missing instance gives 404 Not Found.
  • POST creates a child resource (success is 201 Created with a Location header, and an existing resource gives 409 Conflict) or invokes an operation (200 OK with output, 204 No Content without).
  • PUT creates or replaces the target resource; on the datastore it replaces all contents. It returns 201 Created for a new resource and 204 No Content for a modified one.
  • PATCH with the plain patch merges the body into the target resource; it can create or update, but not delete, and MUST NOT create the target itself.
  • DELETE removes the target and returns 204 No Content.

Query parameters refine requests: content (config, nonconfig or all), depth (1 to 65535 or unbounded), fields, filter for event streams, insert and point for ordered-by user lists, start-time and stop-time for replay, and with-defaults. Each parameter may appear at most once, and an unexpected or repeated one gives 400 Bad Request.

Edit collisions are handled with a last-modified timestamp (If-Unmodified-Since) and an entity-tag (If-Match), which change whenever configuration data below them changes. Responses carry a Cache-Control header and generally SHOULD NOT be cached.
sections.eli5: Asking to read, add, replace, tweak or remove a setting each has its own web request word, and extra bits on the address let you ask for only part of the answer.

sections.title: Notifications and Event Streams
sections.content:
A server MAY support notifications, which keep aspects of NETCONF event notifications (RFC 5277) but are delivered with Server-Sent Events. A client lists available streams with GET on the stream list in the ietf-restconf-monitoring module. Each stream has a name, a description, whether replay is supported, and one or more access entries with an encoding and a location URL.

To subscribe, the client does a GET on the stream's location with Accept: text/event-stream, and the server then treats the connection as an event stream. The start-time and stop-time parameters request replay of earlier events, and filter takes an XPath 1.0 expression to select only the events of interest.

Servers also advertise optional features as capability URIs in the capability leaf-list, which is how RESTCONF is extended without a new protocol version. Version 1 is defined here; a future version would use a different root resource found through a different link relation.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking again and again whether something happened, you leave a connection open and the device sends you news as it happens.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content:
HTTP status codes report success or failure. NETCONF error information is adapted so that a response to a request with a 4xx or 5xx status carries an errors structure, defined by the yang-errors YANG data template. The RFC maps each NETCONF error-tag to a status code, for example in-use, lock-denied, resource-denied, data-exists and data-missing to 409, invalid-value to 400, 404 or 406, and access-denied to 401 or 403.

For 4xx errors other than 403 Forbidden, the server SHOULD send a body in that format, with a Content-Type of application/yang-data plus an optional structured syntax suffix. Responses in the 1xx, 2xx or 3xx range MUST NOT contain error information.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the device replies with a standard number and a short note saying what the problem was and where.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Configuration information is sensitive: it often contains passwords, user names, service descriptions and topology, and sending it unprotected invites eavesdropping and false data injection. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS with TLS as the mandatory-to-implement transport, and access control follows the NETCONF Access Control Model.

Because TLS 1.3 introduces 0-RTT handshakes that can cause security problems for RESTCONF APIs, the RFC RECOMMENDS that servers do not support 0-RTT at all, not even for idempotent requests, until an update to the RFC says otherwise. It also warns that the HTTP authentication schemes vary greatly in strength, and that an unauthorized operation MUST get a 401 error. Security considerations for other YANG modules are left to the documents that define them.
sections.eli5: Device settings are private, so the connection is locked and the device only lets people do what they are allowed to do.
